claims.text: Surface aluminization will produce an adherent Al2O3 scale on the refractory high-entropy alloy.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will improve resistance to high-temperature oxygen attack.
The untreated alloy has insufficient surface aluminum to form a stable protective oxide during high-temperature exposure.
Pack-cementation aluminization will enrich the alloy's near-surface region with aluminum.
The treatment is intended to operate during exposure at 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
The treatment will form a dense, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 scale.
The Al2O3 scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion.
Increasing surface aluminum causes rapid formation of protective Al2O3 during high-temperature exposure.
The Al2O3 scale impedes oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Impeded oxygen diffusion reduces internal oxidation and degradation relative to the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will have lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated alloy under identical exposure conditions.
The treated alloy will have a thinner and more protective oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit a higher oxidation rate, continuous scale growth, and weight gain at 1200°C in air because they form less-protective surface oxides.
The intervention is expected to be effective at 1200°C in air.
The intervention's efficacy may decrease at much higher oxygen pressures or when the base-alloy composition differs substantially from the assumed alloy.
General oxidation principles support the proposed mechanism.
The magnitude of the reduction in oxidation weight gain is uncertain without targeted experimental validation.
Failure to achieve at least a 25% reduction in both oxidation weight gain and oxide-scale thickness relative to untreated controls will falsify the hypothesis.
